description: We are a team of 4 Electrical Engineering students from ITENAS Bandung.  This year we are building an Earth Information Jukebox that turns NASA Earth data into real-time sound, focused on Indonesia. We bring system design, web development, and storytelling skills. We welcome teammates strong in UI design or audio/sound design.
summary: NASA's Earth visualizations are striking, but they rely on sight, which leaves blind and low-vision people out of the story. Earth Jukebox is a free web tool that changes this by turning NASA Earth Information Center images and videos into sound. Users choose a dataset (Night Lights, Sea Surface Currents and Temperature, or Lightning), upload their frames, and press play. A scan line sweeps across the map from left to right, so a place on the left of the image is heard on the left in stereo, while pixel values become pitch and rhythm: brighter city lights, warmer ocean water and denser lightning all sound different. After each frame, a spoken voice explains in plain words what changed since the previous one, and users can move through the map with the arrow keys to hear any single spot. Every control works from the keyboard and speaks its name and new state, and the site supports screen readers, high contrast and larger text. It builds on NASA Black Marble, ECCO2 and ISS Lightning Imaging Sensor visualizations. Values are image-based estimates, not calibrated NASA data.
details:
Earth Jukebox lets people hear NASA Earth data instead of only seeing it. A user picks one of three datasets: Night Lights (city lights at night), Sea Surface Currents and Temperature, or Lightning (flashes seen from the International Space Station). They then upload map images (JPG, PNG, WebP, TIFF or PDF) or a video, and press play. A yellow scan line reads the map from left to right in 32 columns, and each column's position becomes its left-right position in the headphones. Every dataset has its own sound rules. In Night Lights, brighter pixels give higher and louder tones, and darkness is silent. In Sea Surface, each pixel's color is converted to a temperature using NASA's color bar, and warmer water sounds higher. In Lightning, only the yellow dots are read: more dots make a denser drum rhythm, and dots higher on the map sound higher. A "Test sound" button plays the lowest, average and highest tones so listeners learn the scale first.

After every frame, a spoken voice explains what changed compared with the previous frame, so a listener does not have to guess. In Explore mode, arrow keys, mouse or touch move a cursor over the image, and each spot plays its sound and announces its value. Charts, a data table and plain-language conclusions summarize the series, and per-country, continent and ocean summaries can be downloaded as CSV. The whole series can also be played as a short melody and saved as a .wav file.

The benefit is simple: blind and low-vision people, as well as students and teachers, can explore Earth science that was built for the eyes. We hope this makes NASA's Earth Information Center visualizations reachable to more people and more classrooms.

We built Earth Jukebox with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, the Web Audio API for sound (all tones are synthesized in the browser, with no audio files), and the browser's built-in speech synthesis for the voice guide. It also uses pdf.js, UTIF.js, Natural Earth boundaries and the Atkinson Hyperlegible font, and it is hosted on GitHub Pages. No special hardware is needed, only a modern browser, and headphones help for stereo.

What makes it creative is the idea of a scan line that turns a picture into time and stereo space, and the choice to give each dataset its own sonic language. We also considered accessibility from the start: every button, switch and slider speaks its name and new state, all controls work from the keyboard, screen readers receive the same messages when the voice is off, and high contrast and larger text are available. We were careful about honesty too. Values are image-based estimates, not calibrated NASA data, and the country analysis works best on flat world maps. Our next step is listener testing with blind and low-vision users.
